items.title: Concept: learning from what a later snapshot changes
items.body:
Because each snapshot is a full copy, you can open the same file in two snapshots side by side. The journal's study loop asks you to do exactly that: select two adjacent snapshot folders in VS Code and use "Compare Selected".

That is the best way to understand a bug the quizzes describe. Snapshot 07 has a dashboard service; snapshot 11 is about a performance problem; snapshot 12 has another version of the same service. Comparing them shows what was wrong and how it was fixed, in real code rather than in words.

Also read each NOTES.md "Deferred on purpose" section. It lists what the snapshot *knowingly* leaves out (validation, writes, caching rules). A shortcut that is deferred on purpose is still a shortcut, and several quizzes ask what that shortcut costs once the data or traffic gets realistic.

excerpts.quote: 4. Diff against the previous snapshot. In VSCode: select both folders, right-click, then Compare Selected.
10. 10-observability-config - Make runtime behavior visible and environment settings explicit.

items.title: Snapshot 07: one agreement query per company (N+1)
items.body:
`getDashboardSummary` loads all companies with one query. Then, inside `companies.map`, it calls `this.agreements.findByClientCompanyId(company.id)` for **each** company. With 500 companies that is 1 + 500 database round trips: the classic **N+1 query** problem. On seed data (a few in-memory companies) it is instant, so it looks fine. Snapshot 12's version fixes it: one `countByClientIds(...)` call for all ids, then a lookup per company in the returned map.

Why the others are wrong:
- `Promise.all` returns results in the same order as its input, so counts stay matched to companies.
- The code does not load the whole agreements table once; it asks per company.
- `Promise.all` starts all lookups at once (concurrently), but each lookup is still its own query, so it is many round trips, not one.

excerpts.quote: const companies = await this.companies.findAll(); const cards = await Promise.all(companies.map(async (company) => { const agreements = await this.agreements.findByClientCompanyId(company.id);
const agreementCounts = await this.agreements.countByClientIds(companies.map((company) => company.id));

items.title: Snapshot 12: why ?page=abc gives an empty page
items.body:
`Number("abc")` is `NaN`. `Math.max(1, NaN)` is also `NaN`: in JavaScript any math with NaN gives NaN, so the clamp does not help. Then `start = (page - 1) * pageSize` is NaN, and `filtered.slice(NaN, NaN)` treats NaN as 0 for both ends, which gives an empty array. When the response is sent as JSON, `NaN` cannot be written as a number and becomes `null`. So you get no agreements, `page: null`, and a correct `total`, which makes it look like an empty page rather than a bug.

Why the others are wrong:
- `slice(NaN, NaN)` is `slice(0, 0)`, which is empty, not the whole array.
- `Math.max(1, NaN)` is NaN, not 1.
- A TypeScript type does not check request data at runtime; nothing here returns 400.

excerpts.quote: const page = Math.max(1, Number(query.page ?? 1)); const pageSize = Math.min(50, Math.max(5, Number(query.pageSize ?? 10)));
const start = (page - 1) * pageSize; return { agreements: filtered.slice(start, start + pageSize), page, pageSize, total: filtered.length };

items.title: Snapshot 05: how localEntityCode is built from the country
items.body:
`createAgreement` builds the code with `input.workerCountry.slice(0, 2).toUpperCase() + '-EOR-TBD'`. It takes the first two characters of whatever was typed. "Germany" gives "Ge", upper-cased "GE", so the stored code is `GE-EOR-TBD`. Germany's ISO code is DE, so this is wrong. It only works when the input is already a two-letter code. The seed data shows the mismatch: it stores `workerCountry: 'Ireland'` with `localEntityCode: 'IE-EOR-01'`, but "Ireland" through this code would give "IR".

Why the others are wrong:
- No code looks up sequence numbers; the suffix is always `-EOR-TBD`.
- The code is always set on create, never left empty.
- There is no country-name-to-ISO mapping; it just slices the string.

excerpts.quote: localEntityCode: input.workerCountry.slice(0, 2).toUpperCase() + '-EOR-TBD',
workerCountry: 'Ireland', roleTitle: 'Senior Data Analyst', status: 'in_review', startDate: '2026-07-01', localEntityCode: 'IE-EOR-01',

items.title: Snapshot 05: why an unknown company gives not-found
items.body:
`listForClientCompany` first calls `this.companies.findById(clientCompanyId)`. If there is no such company it throws `ApiError.notFound('Client company not found')`. Only when the company exists does it ask the agreement repository. So `company_typo` gets a not-found error, not an empty list. That is better because "this company has no agreements" and "this company does not exist" are different facts. An empty list would hide a typo or a broken link as if everything were fine.

Why the others are wrong:
- No code checks the id's format or prefix; the check is whether the company exists.
- An empty array is what you would get *without* the parent check; this code checks first.
- `findByClientCompanyId` is never reached for a missing company, and nothing here throws a 500.

excerpts.quote: async listForClientCompany(clientCompanyId: string): Promise<WorkAgreementListResponse> { const company = await this.companies.findById(clientCompanyId); if (!company) throw ApiError.notFound('Client company not found'); return { agreements: await this.agreements.findByClientCompanyId(clientCompanyId) }; }

items.title: Snapshot 10: reusing an incoming x-request-id
items.body:
`requestContext` reads the request-id header. If it is present and shorter than 128 characters, it is used as `req.requestId`; otherwise a new `randomUUID()` is made. The id is echoed back in the response header. The benefit: when another service (a gateway, the front end) already gave the request an id, every log line along the way carries the same id, so you can follow one request across hops ("correlation IDs", the skill this snapshot teaches). The accepted risk: only length is checked. Any client can send any value, so ids can be chosen or reused to confuse or spoof logs.

Why the others are wrong:
- A request id says nothing about who the caller is; it is not authentication.
- Saving a `randomUUID` call is not the point, and an empty header is falsy, so it simply gets a new UUID.
- Nothing forces clients to send UUIDs, so uniqueness is not guaranteed.

excerpts.quote: const incoming = req.header(config.requestIdHeader); req.requestId = incoming && incoming.length < 128 ? incoming : randomUUID(); res.setHeader(config.requestIdHeader, req.requestId);
- correlation IDs: snapshots/10-observability-config

items.title: Snapshot 01: what the repository interface buys and costs
items.body:
`ClientCompanyService` receives a `ClientCompanyRepository` through its constructor instead of importing the records array. NOTES 01 records the decision in its usual "chose, rejected, tradeoff" form: the rejected option was routes importing the array directly. The reason given: "The interface makes later persistence swaps visible and testable." The cost given: "It adds a little ceremony before a database exists." So when a real database arrives, only a new repository class is needed, and tests can pass in a fake repository.

Why the others are wrong:
- Nothing in the code adds locks or thread safety.
- Express has no rule that needs an interface for async routes.
- Direct array imports in routes are exactly what the decision *rejected*.

excerpts.quote: - Repository interface first: rejected Direct array imports in routes. The interface makes later persistence swaps visible and testable. It adds a little ceremony before a database exists.
export class ClientCompanyService { constructor(private readonly companies: ClientCompanyRepository) {}

items.title: Concept: controller, service, repository, and hooks on the front end
items.body:
The API follows one layering, set out in the journal's "Architecture conventions":

- A **controller** reads the HTTP request and writes the response.
- A **service** holds the business rules (for example, which status changes are allowed).
- A **repository** hides where data is stored. Here storage is an in-memory array, kept behind a repository so it could be swapped later.
- **Middleware** runs around every request: request ids, errors, auth.
- `packages/shared` holds the DTO types both apps use.

The front end mirrors this: typed API client functions, then **hooks** (like `useApiResource`) that load data into React state, then components that render it.

Why this helps with the quizzes: almost every question is "what does this one layer really do?". Read the method line by line and ask what it returns (a copy or the live object?), what it checks (only a type, or the real value?), and whether it changes React state so the screen re-renders.

excerpts.quote: - Backend: Express-style TypeScript with controllers, services, repositories, middleware, config, and observability modules. - Frontend: React feature folders with typed API clients, auth context, query hooks, reusable UI states, and route-like screen composition. - Shared contracts: packages/shared contains DTOs used by both API and frontend. - Persistence: intentionally in-memory, hidden behind repositories so persistence concerns remain teachable without infrastructure.

readMore.why: Why the repository boundary is introduced so early.
Why services and hooks are pulled out once duplication hurts.

items.title: Start here: one project told as fifteen snapshots
items.body:
This repo teaches a TypeScript/Node API with a React front end (an "operator console" for client companies and their work agreements). It is not one codebase but fifteen: each folder under `snapshots/` is a full copy of the project at one step, from `00-walking-skeleton` to `14-polish-docs`.

Read in this order:

- **README.md**, "How to navigate": start at snapshot 00 and move forward one at a time.
- **LEARNING-JOURNAL.md**: the architecture conventions, the snapshot index (one line of purpose each), the skills-to-snapshot map and the study loop.
- Then each snapshot's **NOTES.md**: its Goal, "Predict before you read", Key decisions (each written as "chose X, rejected Y, tradeoff Z"), "Deferred on purpose" and "Where to look".

The quizzes in this pack visit snapshots 01, 05, 07, 08, 10 and 12. Many ask about a shortcut that works on seed data but breaks later. When a quiz names a snapshot, open *that* snapshot's copy of the file; the same file name in a later snapshot may already be fixed.

excerpts.quote: Each folder under snapshots is a complete copy of the codebase at that moment in the project, not a diff

## Study loop 1. Read the Goal in the snapshot NOTES.md. 2. Answer "Predict before you read" before opening code/. 3. Explore code/ using the "Where to look" pointers. 4. Diff against the previous snapshot. In VSCode: select both folders, right-click, then Compare Selected. 5. Check the Key decisions against your prediction and ask what tradeoff you would have made.

The first NOTES file, showing the format every snapshot uses.

items.title: Snapshot 12: getting an active agreement back to draft
items.body:
`allowedTransitions` lists, for each status, the only statuses it may move to. `active` may go only to `blocked`. `blocked` may go to `draft` or `in_review`. `transition` throws `ApiError(409, 'invalid_status_transition', ...)` for any move not in the list. So active to draft directly gets 409. The allowed path is two steps: active to blocked, then blocked to draft.

Why the others are wrong:
- active is not terminal; it has one exit, to blocked.
- Only `blocked` lists `draft` as a target; other statuses cannot jump straight back.
- Walking backwards is not allowed: no status lists the one before it (for example `ready_for_signature` cannot go to `in_review`).

excerpts.quote: const allowedTransitions: Record<WorkAgreementStatus, WorkAgreementStatus[]> = { draft: ['in_review', 'blocked'], in_review: ['ready_for_signature', 'blocked'], ready_for_signature: ['active', 'blocked'], active: ['blocked'], blocked: ['draft', 'in_review'] }; export class AgreementStatusService { async transition(id: string, nextStatus: WorkAgreementStatus) { const current = await workAgreementRepository.findById(id); if (!current) throw ApiError.notFound('Work agreement not found'); if (!allowedTransitions[current.status].includes(nextStatus)) throw new ApiError(409, 'invalid_status_transition', 'That status transition is not allowed');

items.title: Snapshot 08: why the "optimistic" status change is not visible
items.body:
The query cache is a `Map` created once with `useState(() => new Map())`. `queryClient.set` just calls `cache.set(...)` on that Map. Changing a Map in place does not call any React state setter, so React does not know anything changed and does not re-render. The panel does not read the cache directly anyway: it shows `data` from `useApiResource`, which only changes when `setData` runs. In `changeStatus` that happens at `await resource.reload()`, after the server call returns. So the operator sees the new status only after the save and the reload.

Why the others are wrong:
- Keeping the Map in `useState` does not help: the Map object stays the same, and mutating it is not a state update.
- The rollback only runs in the `catch`, when the server call fails.
- `set` has no subscribers or notifications; it only writes into the Map.

excerpts.quote: const [cache] = useState<Cache>(() => new Map()); const value = useMemo<QueryClientValue>(() => ({ get: (key) => cache.get(serialize(key)) as never, set: (key, value) => { cache.set(serialize(key), value); },

if (current) { queryClient.set(key, { agreements: current.agreements.map((item) => item.id === agreement.id ? { ...item, status } : item) }); } try { await api.updateWorkAgreementStatus(agreement.id, status); } catch (error) { if (current) queryClient.set(key, current); throw error; } await resource.reload();
async function reload() { setIsLoading(true); setError(null); try { setData(await loader());

items.title: Snapshot 10: loadConfig has defaults but no validation
items.body:
Look at the two lines. `port: Number(env.PORT ?? 4100)`: `??` only uses the default when the value is `null` or `undefined`. "http" is a string, so it is kept, and `Number("http")` is `NaN`. `logLevel: (env.LOG_LEVEL as AppConfig['logLevel']) ?? 'info'`: the `as` cast only tells TypeScript to treat the value as one of the allowed levels. It does not check anything at runtime, so "verbose" is stored as is. Nothing throws. The NOTES claim "defaults and validation discoverable", but in this code only the defaults exist.

Why the others are wrong:
- `??` does not replace *invalid* values, only missing ones.
- There is no clamping or mapping code for port or level.
- No code checks the values or throws at startup.

excerpts.quote: port: Number(env.PORT ?? 4100), logLevel: (env.LOG_LEVEL as AppConfig['logLevel']) ?? 'info',
Central config keeps defaults and validation discoverable.

items.title: Snapshot 07: a slow old request overwrites the new company
items.body:
`useApiResource` reruns `reload` whenever the dependencies change. `reload` does `setData(await loader())`: when *any* request finishes, its result is stored. Nothing remembers which request is the current one. So: open A (request A starts, slow), open B (request B starts, fast). B finishes and shows B. Then A finishes and `setData` stores A's data, while the screen is on company B. Last response wins. What is missing is a stale-request guard: an "ignore me" flag set in the effect's cleanup, or an `AbortController` to cancel the old request.

Why the others are wrong:
- `useEffect` does not throw because an older async call is still running.
- `setData` replaces the data; it does not append.
- React does not drop late updates for you; this effect has no cleanup, so the old request still calls `setData`.

excerpts.quote: async function reload() { setIsLoading(true); setError(null); try { setData(await loader()); } catch (caught) { setError(caught); } finally { setIsLoading(false); } } useEffect(() => { reload(); }, dependencies);

items.title: Snapshot 08: why the new agreement is missing after reload
items.body:
`handleSubmit` awaits `api.createWorkAgreement(...)` (so the server did save it), clears the form, and calls `reload()`. `reload` does call the loader again. But the loader in `useCompanyAgreements` begins with `if (cached) return cached;`. The list for this company was cached on the first load, and nothing removed it after the create. So the loader returns the old list without asking the server. The fix is to call `queryClient.invalidate(...)` for that company's key after the create, so the next load really fetches.

Why the others are wrong:
- The panel shows `data?.agreements` without filtering by status.
- The create is awaited (`await api.createWorkAgreement`), so it is not fire-and-forget.
- `reload` does call the loader; the problem is the loader's cache check.

excerpts.quote: async function handleSubmit(event: FormEvent) { event.preventDefault(); await api.createWorkAgreement({ clientCompanyId, workerName, workerCountry, roleTitle, startDate }); setWorkerName(''); setWorkerCountry(''); setRoleTitle(''); setStartDate(''); await reload(); }

const resource = useApiResource(async () => { const key = [...agreementKeys.byCompany(companyId)]; const cached = queryClient.get<Awaited<ReturnType<typeof api.listAgreementsForCompany>>>(key); if (cached) return cached; const result = await api.listAgreementsForCompany(companyId); queryClient.set(key, result); return result; }, [companyId]);
invalidate: (prefix) => { const serializedPrefix = JSON.stringify(prefix).slice(0, -1); for (const key of cache.keys()) if (key.startsWith(serializedPrefix)) cache.delete(key); }

items.title: Snapshot 10: what the log keeps about an unexpected error
items.body:
In `errorMiddleware`, an `ApiError` takes the first branch. A TypeError is not an ApiError, so it reaches `logger.error({ message: 'unexpected api error', requestId: req.requestId, errorName: error?.name })`. The logger writes exactly the fields it is given as one JSON line, with level "error". So the line has the requestId (correlation works) and `errorName: "TypeError"`, but not the error's message ("Cannot read properties...") or its stack. The client gets only "Unexpected server error" and the requestId.

Why the others are wrong:
- Unexpected errors *are* logged, at level error; ApiErrors are logged as warnings.
- `logger.error` receives a small object, not the Error itself, so the message and stack are never passed in.
- The 500 body has a generic message and no stack.

excerpts.quote: logger.error({ message: 'unexpected api error', requestId: req.requestId, errorName: error?.name }); res.status(500).json({ error: { code: 'internal_error', message: 'Unexpected server error', requestId: req.requestId } });
function write(event: LogEvent) { console.log(JSON.stringify({ timestamp: new Date().toISOString(), service: 'atlas-api', ...event })); }

items.title: Snapshot 01: findById hands out the stored object itself
items.body:
`findAll` returns `[...clientCompanyRecords]`, a new array (though it still holds the same company objects). `findById` returns `clientCompanyRecords.find(...)`, which is the very object stored in the in-memory array, not a copy. In JavaScript, objects are passed by reference: `c` and the array entry are the same object. So `c.legalName = 'Draft'` changes the "stored" record at once, with no save call. A real database would not behave like this, which is why later repositories return copies (`{ ...agreement }`).

Why the others are wrong:
- Nothing freezes the records, so assignment works.
- An `async` function's result is not cloned; the Promise resolves with the same object.
- Only `findAll` spreads (and only the array); `findById` does not copy at all.

excerpts.quote: async findAll() { return [...clientCompanyRecords]; } async findById(id: string) { return clientCompanyRecords.find((company) => company.id === id) ?? null; }
async findById(id: string) { const agreement = workAgreementRecords.find((candidate) => candidate.id === id); return agreement ? { ...agreement } : null; }
